title: What a trust is: settlor, trustee, beneficiary, trust property
summary: A trust is a relationship, not a company: one person holds property for the benefit of others under binding rules. Getting the three roles and the property right at the start decides whether the trust works at all.
body:
Bottom line. A trust is not a company and not a contract. It is a relationship in which one person holds property for the benefit of other people, under rules that a court will enforce. Mr Shabazz, if you can name the settlor, the trustee, the beneficiaries and the property, and show that each one is real, you understand most of what makes a trust valid.

In plain English

Picture a box of assets. Someone puts the assets in the box. That person is the settlor. Someone else holds the key and decides what happens to the box. That person is the trustee. A third group of people are the ones the box exists for. They are the beneficiaries. The assets in the box are the trust property, which lawyers also call the corpus or the capital.

The key idea is the split between legal ownership and benefit. The trustee is the legal owner. The trustee's name is on the share register or the bank account. But the trustee may not use the property for himself. He must use it for the beneficiaries, and only in the ways the trust document allows. That document is usually called the trust deed or trust indenture.

A trust is not a separate legal person the way a corporation is. It cannot sign anything. The trustees sign, as trustees. For income tax purposes in Canada, a trust is treated as if it were an individual and files its own return, but in general law it remains a relationship between people.

The framework

Lawyers test whether a trust exists using the three certainties, a common law rule that Canadian courts apply. All three must be present.

  1. Certainty of intention. The settlor must clearly intend to create a trust, not to make a gift, a loan or a wish. Words like "I hope my son will share" usually fail. Words like "my trustee shall hold" usually pass.
  2. Certainty of subject matter. The property must be identified. "Some of my shares" fails. "One hundred common shares of a named company" passes.
  3. Certainty of objects. The beneficiaries must be identifiable, or the class must be described clearly enough that a trustee can tell whether a given person is in it or out of it.

Then there are four practical questions a professional asks:

  1. Who settled it, and with what? Settlors often use a single coin or a small amount of cash. The settlor is usually chosen so that the settlor is not a beneficiary and never gets anything back. That point matters for tax, which a later lesson covers.
  2. Who are the trustees, and how many? More than one trustee is common, so that a death or a dispute does not freeze the trust.
  3. Who can benefit, and on what terms? Fixed shares, or discretion, or a mix.
  4. When does it end? Every trust needs an end date or an end event.

Two more terms. Income is what the property earns, such as dividends or rent. Capital is the property itself. A deed can treat the two differently, for example income to one group and capital to another.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A developer wants his family to share in the growth of a new operating company without each family member holding shares directly. His aunt, who will never benefit, gives a hypothetical $100 bill to two trustees, the developer and a long-time accountant friend. The deed says the trustees hold the bill "in trust" for the developer's spouse and children, as a defined class, and may pay income or capital to any of them. That bill is the trust property.

The trustees then use trust money, borrowed from an arm's length lender or properly documented, to subscribe for hypothetical 1,000 common shares of the operating company at $0.01 each, a hypothetical $10 total. The share register shows the trustees as owners, described as trustees of the named trust. Ten years later the hypothetical company is worth $2,000,000. That growth sits inside the trust, for the class of beneficiaries, rather than in any one person's name.

Notice the order: settle first, with the settlor's own property, then the trust buys. If the developer had settled the trust with his own money, or the trust had bought the shares with money he gave it, the result could be very different for tax.

Professional Sign-Off Required: lawyer (trusts) and tax advisor (CPA)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is treating the trust as paperwork that can be filled in later. A trust that exists only on paper, with no property actually transferred, no signed deed at the right date, and no trustee decisions recorded, may be a sham. A sham is an arrangement in which the documents say one thing and the parties intend another. A court or a tax authority can disregard it. The second beginner mistake is having the settlor also be a beneficiary or a trustee who controls the money he put in. That can undo the planning.

How you will use it

As a developer, you will meet trusts in three places. First, a family trust may own shares of a holding company, so growth is shared across a family. Second, a lender or partner will ask who stands behind the trust and who the trustees are, because the trustees sign. Third, an estate plan may create trusts on death. In each case, start by drawing a simple diagram: settlor, trustees, beneficiaries, property, end date. If you cannot fill every box with a real name or a real asset, the structure is not ready. Bring that diagram to counsel. It turns a long first meeting into a short one, and it lets the lawyer spend time on the deed's terms rather than on finding the facts.
checklist: Name the settlor, and confirm the settlor will never be a beneficiary
Name at least two trustees, and decide who replaces them
Describe the beneficiary class clearly enough to test any person in or out
Identify the exact trust property and transfer it on the deed date
State an end date or end event in the deed
Keep the signed deed and a record of the first transfer in one file
Record trustee decisions in writing from day one

selftest.q: A developer signs a trust deed naming his children as beneficiaries, but he never transfers any property to the trustees, and later the trust buys shares with money he lends it informally. What is wrong?
selftest.a: Certainty of subject matter fails at the start because no property was settled, so there may be no trust at all. Even if a trust exists later, funding it with the developer's own informal money can link him to the property and change the tax result. A professional would want a proper settlement by a non-beneficiary settlor, then documented funding.

apply: Draw a one-page diagram of any trust you have or plan: settlor, trustees, beneficiaries, property and end date. Mark every box you cannot fill with a real name or asset.
sources: The three certainties are a long-standing common law rule (Knight v Knight, 1840, English Court of Chancery), applied by Canadian courts. The treatment of a trust as an individual for tax is in the Income Tax Act (Canada), subsection 104(2). Confirm the current text of both before relying on them. Education only, not legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: lawyer (trusts) and tax advisor (CPA)

title: Discretionary family trusts: what discretion buys and costs
summary: A discretionary trust lets trustees decide later who receives income or capital, which buys flexibility and some protection. It costs control, administration and, today, much of the old tax benefit.
body:
Bottom line. In a discretionary trust, the trustees decide later who gets what, inside rules set by the deed. Mr Shabazz, that flexibility is valuable for family planning and creditor distance, but it is paid for with loss of personal control, real administration, and tax rules that now remove much of the old income-splitting benefit.

In plain English

A fixed trust says in advance who gets what share. For example, each of three children gets one third. A discretionary trust does not fix shares. It names a class of possible beneficiaries and lets the trustees choose, each year or at a chosen time, who receives income and who receives capital, and how much. Nobody in the class owns a defined slice until the trustees decide.

That is the whole trade. Because no beneficiary owns a fixed slice, there is less to seize if a beneficiary is sued or divorced, and the trustees can respond to how life turns out. But the person who created the plan no longer simply owns the assets. Decisions must be made properly, by the trustees, and recorded.

The framework

Weigh discretion against its costs, item by item.

  1. Flexibility. Trustees can favour a child who needs help, skip one who does not, and wait until a child is mature before giving capital.
  2. Creditor distance. A beneficiary usually has only a hope of receiving something, not a property right. That often makes the interest hard for the beneficiary's creditor to reach. It is not a guarantee, and it does not protect the settlor from his own creditors if he moved property in to defeat them.
  3. Growth shifting. Future growth in value can accumulate in the trust rather than in one person's estate. This is often called an estate freeze, covered in later lessons.
  4. Control cost. The trustees control, not the founder personally. Founders often serve as one trustee, but must then act as a trustee, for the beneficiaries, not for themselves.
  5. Administration cost. Annual tax filings, trustee resolutions, accounts, and professional fees every year.
  6. Tax cost. Canada restricts the old practice of paying income to low-income family members. The tax on split income rules in section 120.4 of the Income Tax Act (Canada) can tax certain amounts at the top personal rate. Attribution rules can also send income back to the person who funded the trust. A trust also faces a deemed sale of its capital property every 21 years, under subsection 104(4).
  7. Reporting cost. Trusts now face expanded reporting of who the settlors, trustees and beneficiaries are. The exact thresholds and exemptions have changed in recent years. [unverified — confirm independently]

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A family trust owns all the common shares of a holding company. In one year the holding company pays a hypothetical $100,000 dividend to the trust. The beneficiaries are the founder's spouse and two adult children, one a student and one working in the business.

In the old approach, a family might have paid the dividend out to the student to use a low tax rate. Today, the trustees and their advisor must ask whether the tax on split income rules apply to each person. Those rules have exclusions, for example for certain people who actively work in the business or who are over a certain age with qualifying shares. The answers decide whether paying the student saves tax or simply costs the top rate. [unverified — confirm independently]

Suppose the advisor concludes that paying the working child is excluded from the rules and paying the student is not. The trustees meet, consider each beneficiary's needs, and pass a written resolution to allocate the income to the working child and to pay it before the deadline in the deed. They keep the minutes. The discretion was used, and used properly.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA) and lawyer (trusts)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is believing that discretion means the founder can do whatever he likes. A trustee who always does what one person says, or who never actually considers the beneficiaries, may not be exercising discretion at all. A court can treat that as a breach of trust, or a tax authority can argue the trust is not what it claims. A second mistake is making allocations after the year ends without a resolution that the deed and the tax rules require to be made in time.

How you will use it

As a developer, think of a discretionary trust as a tool for long horizons, not for this year's tax bill. Use it when you want growth in a holding company to belong to a family over decades, with flexibility to adjust. Before you set one up, ask three questions in writing: who will be the trustees in twenty years, who pays for the annual administration, and what does the trust need to do before its 21-year date. When you sit with your advisor, ask them to show you the tax result of an allocation before the trustees vote, not after. That keeps decisions deliberate and recorded, which is what protects the structure.
checklist: Decide whether you truly need discretion, or a simpler fixed arrangement
List every possible beneficiary class and confirm the deed allows each one
Get a written tax on split income analysis before each allocation
Pass trustee resolutions before the deadlines set by the deed and tax rules
Budget the annual cost of filings, accounts and professional fees
Diary the trust's 21-year date on the day it is settled
Keep minutes showing the trustees considered each beneficiary

selftest.q: A founder is one of three trustees of a discretionary trust. Each year he tells the other two trustees who should get the income, and they sign whatever he prepares without discussion. What risks does this create?
selftest.a: The other trustees are not exercising their own discretion, so the decisions may be a breach of trust and could be challenged by a beneficiary. It can also support an argument that the trust is controlled by one person and not operating as a genuine trust. Each trustee must actually consider the beneficiaries and the deed, and the minutes should show that.

apply: Write down who you would want as trustees of a family trust today, who replaces each, and who would pay the yearly administration cost.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): section 120.4 (tax on split income) and subsection 104(4) (deemed disposition every 21 years). Trust reporting rules and their exemptions have changed recently and are tagged unverified; confirm with the CRA's current guidance. Education only, not advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA) and lawyer (trusts)

title: Trustee duties and the trust deed: powers, protectors, replacement
summary: Trustees owe strict duties of loyalty, care and even-handedness, and they can only do what the deed and the law allow. The deed's powers, any protector role and the replacement mechanism decide whether the trust keeps working for decades.
body:
Bottom line. A trustee is held to a very high standard and may only act within the powers the deed and the law give. Mr Shabazz, a well-drafted deed spells out those powers, names who can watch over the trustees, and says exactly how a trustee is replaced, so the trust survives deaths, disputes and time.

In plain English

A trustee is like a manager who can never put himself first. The law calls this a fiduciary relationship. A fiduciary is a person who must act for someone else's benefit, not his own. Trustees must be loyal, careful, fair between beneficiaries, and honest in their records.

The trust deed is the rulebook. It says what the trustees may do, such as invest, borrow, lend, or vote shares. Where the deed is silent, the general law fills the gap. In Alberta, a statute called the Trustee Act sets default rules, and other provinces have their own. [unverified — confirm independently]

A protector is an optional extra person named in the deed who can approve or block certain trustee decisions, or replace trustees. Protectors are common in some countries and less common in Canada. Their role is only what the deed gives them.

The framework

The core trustee duties are:

  1. Loyalty. No conflict of interest and no profit from the role without permission. A trustee who sells his own property to the trust, or buys from it, needs clear authority.
  2. Care. Act with the care of a prudent person managing someone else's property. Many provinces now apply a prudent investor standard to investments.
  3. Even-handedness. Treat beneficiaries fairly, including between those who get income now and those who get capital later.
  4. Act personally. A trustee may hire experts but generally may not hand over the core decisions, unless the deed or statute allows.
  5. Account. Keep records and be ready to show beneficiaries how the property was managed.
  6. Act unanimously, unless the deed says otherwise. The general rule for private trusts is that trustees act together. Many deeds allow majority decisions instead.

Then read the deed for five clauses:

  1. Powers. Invest, borrow, guarantee, lend to beneficiaries, hold shares of a private company, and vote them.
  2. Decisions. Unanimous or majority, quorum, and written resolutions.
  3. Protector, if any. What the protector can veto, and whether the protector also owes fiduciary duties.
  4. Replacement. Who may appoint a new trustee, how a trustee resigns, and what happens on death or incapacity.
  5. Exculpation and indemnity. Whether a trustee is excused for honest mistakes, and paid back for proper expenses.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A family trust holds the shares of a holding company, which owns a hypothetical $4,000,000 of investment real estate. The deed names two trustees: the founder and his brother. It requires unanimous decisions. It names no protector and says only that "a new trustee may be appointed by the trustees."

The brother dies. The founder is now the only trustee, but the deed requires two trustees to act. He cannot appoint a replacement alone if the deed requires the trustees, plural, to do it. The trust cannot sign the renewal of a hypothetical $1,500,000 mortgage on time. The founder must now apply to court for an order appointing a new trustee, which costs time and fees and puts the financing at risk.

A better deed would have named a successor trustee in advance, let a sole surviving trustee appoint a co-trustee, allowed majority decisions, and perhaps named a protector with power to appoint trustees if the trustees could not act.

Professional Sign-Off Required: lawyer (trusts)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is choosing trustees for friendship and never reading the replacement clause. Trustees die, fall out, move abroad and lose capacity. A deed that cannot replace a trustee without going to court is a deed that will freeze at the worst moment. A second mistake is a trustee lending trust money to his own company at a friendly rate. That is a conflict of interest, and the trustee can be made to repay any loss.

How you will use it

As a developer, you will often be both a trustee and a person who does business with the trust's company. Keep the two roles apart. When the trust or its company deals with you or your other companies, record the reason, get the deed's authority, and where needed get the other trustee's written approval. Before any major financing, check that the trustees can sign, that there are enough of them, and that the deed gives power to borrow and to grant security. Lenders will ask for the deed and for evidence of trustee authority. Have a short certificate ready that lists the current trustees and quotes the powers clause. It saves days at closing. Finally, ask whoever you choose as a trustee to read the deed before they agree to serve. A trustee who understands the duties is less likely to sign something carelessly, and less likely to resign in a hurry when the work becomes real.
checklist: Read the powers clause and confirm power to borrow, guarantee and grant security
Confirm whether decisions are unanimous or majority
Name a successor trustee and a way to appoint one without going to court
Decide whether a protector is needed and limit the protector's powers in writing
Record any dealing between a trustee and the trust, with the authority used
Keep a current trustee certificate ready for lenders
Review the deed every few years and after any trustee change

selftest.q: A deed requires unanimous trustee decisions and has no successor clause. One of two trustees moves overseas and stops answering. The trust must refinance in sixty days. What are the options and what should have been in the deed?
selftest.a: The remaining trustee may not be able to act alone, so the options are to persuade the absent trustee to resign and consent to a replacement, or to apply to court to appoint a new trustee. The deed should have allowed majority decisions or a sole surviving trustee to act, named successors, and given a person power to remove and replace an unresponsive trustee.

apply: Find the replacement clause in any trust deed you are part of and write one sentence describing what happens if a trustee dies tomorrow.
sources: Fiduciary duties of trustees are common law principles applied by Canadian courts. Provincial Trustee Acts, including Alberta's, set default powers and investment standards; their current sections are tagged unverified and should be confirmed in the official statute. Education only, not legal advice.

title: Trusts and tax: attribution and the deemed disposition clock (concepts)
summary: Canada's attribution rules can send trust income back to the person who funded it, and every 21 years a trust is treated as selling its capital property. Planning means knowing both rules before the trust is funded and well before the clock runs out.
body:
Bottom line. Two tax ideas shape almost every Canadian family trust. Attribution rules can tax trust income in the hands of the person who funded it, and a 21-year rule treats the trust as selling its capital property at fair market value. Mr Shabazz, know both before money goes in, and diary the second on the day the trust is born.

In plain English

Attribution means the tax law pretends that income belongs to someone other than the person who received it. The aim is to stop a high earner from giving or lending property to a family member so that the family member pays tax at a lower rate. If the rules apply, the person who supplied the property pays the tax.

A deemed disposition is a sale that the tax law pretends happened, even though nothing was sold. On a deemed disposition at fair market value, which is the price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller, any gain since the property was acquired becomes taxable.

The 21-year rule exists so that property cannot sit in a trust for generations without its growth ever being taxed.

The framework

These are concepts only. The rules are long and have many exceptions.

  1. Spousal attribution. Under section 74.1 of the Income Tax Act (Canada), income from property transferred or lent to a spouse or common-law partner, or to certain minors, can be attributed back to the transferor. Section 74.2 does similar work for capital gains on property transferred to a spouse.
  2. Attribution through a trust. Section 74.3 applies these rules where the property passes through a trust.
  3. Corporate attribution. Section 74.4 can apply where property is transferred to a corporation and a spouse or certain minors benefit.
  4. Loans. Subsection 56(4.1) can attribute income from certain low-interest or interest-free loans to non-arm's length individuals. A loan at the prescribed rate, with interest actually paid on time, is a common way to avoid attribution. The prescribed rate changes each quarter. [unverified — confirm independently]
  5. Reversionary trusts. Subsection 75(2) can attribute income and gains to a person who contributed property to a trust if that property can revert to him, or if he controls who gets it. This is why the settlor is usually someone who will never benefit, and why the founder does not personally fund the trust.
  6. Tax on split income. Section 120.4 can tax certain amounts paid through a trust to family members at the top rate.
  7. The 21-year rule. Subsection 104(4) deems a trust to dispose of its capital property at fair market value on each 21-year anniversary. A common planning step is for the trustees, before that date, to distribute capital property to Canadian-resident beneficiaries, often on a tax-deferred basis under subsection 107(2). Distributions to non-resident beneficiaries are generally not tax-deferred in the same way. [unverified — confirm independently]

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A family trust was settled in year 1 and bought shares of a holding company for a hypothetical $100. By year 20 those shares are worth a hypothetical $3,000,000.

If the trust does nothing, on the 21st anniversary it is treated as selling the shares for $3,000,000. The hypothetical gain is $2,999,900. The trust may owe tax on that gain even though it received no cash. It may have to borrow or force the company to pay a dividend to fund the tax.

Instead, in year 19 the trustees and their advisors review the plan. Two beneficiaries are resident in Canada and one has moved abroad. The trustees consider distributing shares to the Canadian residents before the anniversary, where the deed allows. That generally passes the shares at the trust's cost, deferring the gain to the beneficiaries. The non-resident beneficiary needs separate analysis because the deferral may not apply. The advisors also check that the original funding did not trigger section 75(2), because that could have changed the tax on gains over the whole period.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA, with trust experience) and lawyer (trusts)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is the founder putting his own money into the trust, or lending to it at no interest, to buy the first shares. That can trigger attribution or section 75(2) and undo years of planning. The second mistake is forgetting the 21-year date. Nobody sends a reminder, and the deadline does not move because the trust has no cash.

How you will use it

As a developer, ask two questions before any trust is funded. Where does the first dollar come from, and can any of it ever come back to the person who supplied it? Get the answer in writing from a tax advisor. Then put the 21-year date in your own calendar with reminders at year 15, 18 and 20. Three years is a sensible window to decide whether to distribute, restructure or accept the tax. If beneficiaries may move abroad, raise it early, because residence changes the options. Treat these rules as a design constraint, like a setback line on a site plan: you draw within them from the start, rather than discovering them at the end.
checklist: Confirm the settlor is a non-beneficiary who supplies their own property
Never fund a trust with the founder's own money without written tax advice
Document any loan to the trust and pay interest at the prescribed rate on time
Ask whether section 75(2) could apply to any contribution
Diary the 21-year date with reminders at years 15, 18 and 20
Track each beneficiary's country of residence every year
Get a tax on split income review before each allocation

selftest.q: A founder lends his family trust a hypothetical $500,000 interest-free so it can buy investments, and the trust allocates the investment income to his adult children. What tax issues should he raise with his advisor?
selftest.a: An interest-free loan to a trust for family members can trigger attribution of the income back to him under the loan rules in subsection 56(4.1), and possibly other attribution rules, and the allocations may also face tax on split income. A loan at the prescribed rate with interest actually paid, or a different structure, may be needed. He should also confirm that section 75(2) does not apply.

apply: If you have a trust, find its settlement date, add 21 years, and put reminders in your calendar at years 15, 18 and 20.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): sections 74.1, 74.2, 74.3 and 74.4 (attribution), subsection 56(4.1) (loans), subsection 75(2) (reversionary trusts), section 120.4 (tax on split income), subsection 104(4) (21-year deemed disposition) and subsection 107(2) (capital distributions). The prescribed rate and the treatment of non-resident beneficiaries are tagged unverified. Read the current Act and CRA guidance. Education only, not tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA, with trust experience) and lawyer (trusts)
